blocks.title: Phase
blocks.text: The angle theta = wt, which specifies both the displacement and the direction of motion of a point oscillating in S.H.M., is called its phase. Phase shows the state of motion of an oscillator.

In general the displacement is written x = xo cos(wt + phi) (14.18). The time-varying quantity (wt + phi) is the phase of the motion; it describes the state of motion at a given time. The constant phi is the phase constant (or phase angle); its value depends on the displacement and velocity of the particle at t = 0. The quantity phi also gives the phase difference between the states of motion of two oscillators.

items: phi = 0: x = xo cos(wt). At t = 0, T/2 and T (theta = 0, pi and 2 pi) the point is at an extreme position; at t = T/4 and 3T/4 (theta = pi/2 and 3 pi/2) it is at the mean position.
phi = 90 degrees: x = xo cos(wt + 90 degrees). At t = 0, T/2 and T the point is at the mean position; at T/4 and 3T/4 it is at an extreme.
phi = 180 degrees: x = xo cos(wt + 180 degrees) = -xo cos(wt): the motion is the exact opposite of the first.

blocks.text: When the phase difference between two oscillating systems is 180 degrees they are said to oscillate out of phase; when it is 0 or 360 degrees they oscillate in phase.

blocks.alt: Three graphs of displacement x against time t over one period, with T/4, T/2, 3T/4 and T marked. phi = 0 (blue): a cosine starting at +xo. phi = 90 degrees (purple): starts at zero and moves to -xo first. phi = 180 degrees (red): starts at -xo, the mirror image of the first graph.
blocks.caption: x = xo cos(wt + phi) for phi = 0, 90 and 180 degrees (original graphs after Fig 14.8).
blocks.long_description: The three oscillators have the same amplitude and period; only their starting points in the cycle differ. The first and third are always on opposite sides of O: they are 180 degrees out of phase.

blocks.title: Captions of Fig 14.8
blocks.text: In the book, Fig 14.8 (b) is captioned phi = 0 and Fig 14.8 (c) phi = 90 degrees; from the text they should be phi = 90 degrees and phi = 180 degrees. The text's 'theta = 0, pi and 2' should read 0, pi and 2 pi.

A 0.5 kg mass is attached to a spring with k = 200 N m^-1. It is displaced 0.2 m from equilibrium and released from rest. Assuming S.H.M., find its displacement, velocity and acceleration at t = 0.5 s. Solution: w = square root of (k/m) = square root of (200/0.5) = 20 rad s^-1, and since it starts from rest at the extreme, x = xo cos(wt). At t = 0.5 s, wt = 10 rad, and cos(10 rad) = -0.839, sin(10 rad) = -0.544. Displacement: x = 0.2 x (-0.839) = -0.168 m. Velocity: v = -xo w sin(wt) = -(0.2)(20)(-0.544) = +2.18 m s^-1. Acceleration: a = -w^2 x = -(400)(-0.168) = +67.1 m s^-2.

blocks.title: Signs in Example 14.4
blocks.text: The book treats cos(10) as +0.839 and sin(10) as +0.544, giving x = +0.168 m, v = 2.176 m s^-1 and a = -67.12 m s^-2. With the angle in radians, cos(10) and sin(10) are both negative, so the mass is on the other side of O: x = -0.168 m, v = +2.18 m s^-1 and a = +67.1 m s^-2 (the magnitudes are unchanged). Part (c) is also printed as 't = 0.05 s'. Flagged for review.

blocks.prompt: Two identical pendulums swing so that one is at its right-hand extreme when the other is at its left-hand extreme. What is their phase difference?
blocks.explanation: 180 degrees (pi radians): they are out of phase.

items: Phase (wt + phi) gives the state of motion; phi is the phase constant.
Phase difference 0 or 360 degrees: in phase; 180 degrees: out of phase.
